topics.benchmark_preservation: The approved design reference, prior topic artifacts and canonical Political Theory owners remain immutable.

panels.panel_title: Method, Approach and the Methodological Turn
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Method, Approach and the Methodological Turn
[1] Method means procedure of inquiry; approach means procedure plus criteria for
selecting problems and data. (PDF pp.108-109)
v
[2] Gauba shows that disputes in political theory are often methodological before they
become ideological. (PDF pp.108-122)
v
[3] It introduces the major traditional approaches—philosophical, historical, legal and
institutional—and the later behavioural turn. (PDF pp.112-122)
v
[4] In Optional answers, clean method language often separates average answers from
high-scoring answers.
v
[5] Traditional and contemporary are historical labels; they do not exactly coincide
with normative and empirical. (PDF pp.109-110)
v
[6] Empirical inquiry studies what can be observed and tested; normative inquiry judges
what ought to be preferred or prescribed. (PDF pp.110-112)
v
SYNTHESIS -> Method, Approach and the Methodological Turn is best presented through its
central claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.

panels.panel_title: Empirical and Normative Inquiry by Content
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Empirical and Normative Inquiry by Content
[1] He clarifies that empirical vs normative turns on the content of the claim, not just
the grammatical presence of "is" or "ought". (PDF pp.110-112)
v
[2] He then warns that traditional/contemporary and normative/empirical are not
identical pairs. (PDF pp.109-110)
v
[3] Gauba begins by separating method from approach so that students do not confuse
tools of inquiry with frames of inquiry. (PDF pp.108-109)
v
[4] The traditional approaches are then outlined: philosophical, historical, legal and
institutional. (PDF pp.112-117)
v
[5] The contemporary shift is marked by behaviouralism, post-behaviouralism and several
models of political analysis. (PDF pp.117-134)
v
[6] The chapter's deeper message is integrative: political science is weakened both by
value-blind technique and by unsupported moral assertion.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Empirical and Normative Inquiry by Content is best presented through its central
claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Traditional Approaches and Their Thinkers
[1] Method vs approach: methods obtain and use data; approaches decide which questions
and data count as relevant. (PDF pp.108-109)
v
[2] Traditional vs contemporary: the first cluster is associated with philosophy,
history, law and institutions, while the second focuses more on process, behaviour
and analysis models. (PDF pp.109-110, 117-118)
v
[3] Empirical vs normative: empirical asks what is observable and testable; normative
asks what is right, just or preferable. (PDF pp.110-112)
v
[4] Form vs content: a sentence using "ought" may still be empirical if it states an
instrumentally testable condition, while a sentence using "is" may still be
normative if it defines a value like justice. (PDF pp.110-111)
v
[5] Pure science vs relevance: behaviouralism stressed reliable inquiry;
post-behaviouralism added action and public responsibility. (PDF pp.121-122)
v
SYNTHESIS -> Traditional Approaches and Their Thinkers is best presented through its central
claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Illustrations, Comparison and Trap Repair
[1] "Everybody ought to vote if democracy is to work" is empirical in content because
its claim can be checked against political functioning. (PDF pp.110-111)
v
[2] "Justice is treating equals equally..." is normative in content even though it
appears in the form of an "is" statement. (PDF p.110)
v
[3] Legal analysis of Indian politics would ask what constitutional provisions authorize
institutions and actions. (PDF pp.115-116)
v
[4] Institutional analysis would map legislature, executive, judiciary, parties and
their formal relations. (PDF pp.116-117)
v
[5] Behavioural analysis of the same political scene would ask how voters, leaders,
parties and interest groups actually behave.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Illustrations, Comparison and Trap Repair is best presented through its central
claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Boundaries, Revision and Source Discipline
[1] Primary source used directly: Gauba, Ch.4, especially PDF pp.108-122 for basic
distinctions and the behavioural/post-behavioural debate.
v
[2] Behaviouralism: scientific study of actual behaviour, eight key tenets, micro-level
reliability. (PDF pp.118-121)
v
[3] Post-behaviouralism: relevance, action and responsible value concern without
discarding scientific gains. (PDF pp.121-122)
v
[4] Best answer line: political inquiry needs both disciplined evidence and defensible
value judgment.
v
[5] This basic file reconstructs behaviouralism's eight tenets and all five analytical
models (systems, structural-functional, communications/cybernetic, decision-making,
Marxian) directly, so it is independently sufficient for full-mark answers; the
advanced companion adds further comparative depth and answer-engine prompts.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Boundaries, Revision and Source Discipline is best presented through its central
claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Behaviouralism's Eight Tenets
[1] Exam use: naming these eight in order and pairing two or three with a one-line
illustration (e.g. quantification → voting-behaviour surveys; integration →
borrowing psychology for leadership studies) earns more marks than a vague
"behaviouralism is scientific" line.
v
[2] Techniques — rigorous tools and methods (surveys, statistics, sampling) are used to
acquire and interpret data.
v
[3] Quantification — precision through measurement and quantification wherever the data
meaningfully allow it.
v
[4] Values — an analytic separation is drawn between empirical explanation and ethical
evaluation (value-neutrality as method, not indifference).
v
[5] Systematization — research and theory are interdependent; data collection is guided
by, and in turn refines, theory.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Behaviouralism's Eight Tenets is best presented through its central claim, causal
logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
Post-Behavioural Relevance and Action
[1] Post-behaviouralism: A corrective within behavioural political science stressing
relevance, action and concern for values.
v
[2] David Easton: Gives both the behavioural framework and the later post-behavioural
call for relevance and action.
v
[3] Post-behaviouralism, associated with Easton's own self-correction, retains the
scientific gains of behaviouralism (rigour, verification, technique) but adds two
demands: relevance — political science must address urgent public problems (war,
poverty, discrimination, injustice) rather than only tractable micro-questions — and
action — intellectuals bear responsibility to apply knowledge for social betterment,
not merely to accumulate value-neutral findings. (PDF pp.121-122)
v
[4] Post-behavioural: Science should remain rigorous but also relevant, action-oriented
and attentive to value-construction.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Post-Behavioural Relevance and Action is best presented through its central
claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.

panels.panel_title: Easton and Almond: Systems and Structural Functions
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Easton and Almond: Systems and Structural Functions
[1] Gabriel Almond — structural-functional approach: every political system, regardless
of its formal constitution, must perform certain universal functions (political
socialization and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation,
rule-making, rule-application, rule-adjudication, and communication); these
functions can be performed by different structures in different systems (e.g.
interest articulation via parties in one system, via kinship or patron-client
networks in another).
v
[2] Reconstruct at least two analytical models (e.g. Easton's systems model and Almond's
structural-functional approach, or Deutsch's cybernetic model and the Marxian
approach) with claim→evidence→significance→limit each, plus the comparison table's
logic.
v
[3] Structural-functional (Almond): Functions performed by variable structures
v
[4] Limit: functionalism's assumption that systems tend toward equilibrium risks a
conservative bias (downplaying conflict and structural change), and in practice
often measured non-Western systems against a Western liberal-democratic benchmark
despite the framework's own claim to be structure-neutral.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Easton and Almond: Systems and Structural Functions is best presented through its
central claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.

panels.panel_title: Deutsch, Decision-Making, Marxian Analysis and Model Comparison
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Deutsch, Decision-Making, Marxian Analysis and Model Comparison
[1] Reconstruct at least two analytical models (e.g. Easton's systems model and Almond's
structural-functional approach, or Deutsch's cybernetic model and the Marxian
approach) with claim→evidence→significance→limit each, plus the comparison table's
logic.
v
[2] Evidence/mechanism: decision-making frameworks (e.g. those used in foreign-policy
analysis) break a decision into stages — problem recognition, search for
alternatives, evaluation, choice, and implementation — and examine the internal
organisational context of the deciding body.
v
[3] Karl Deutsch — communication/cybernetic approach: government functions like a
steering mechanism, and politics can be modelled on cybernetics (the science of
communication and control) — decision-making depends on the flow of information
through communication channels, with feedback loops correcting the system's course
toward its goals.
v
[4] Evidence/mechanism: analysis of who owns and controls the means of production is
used to explain apparently neutral political institutions (law, bureaucracy, even
ideology) as expressions of underlying class interest.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Deutsch, Decision-Making, Marxian Analysis and Model Comparison is best presented
through its central claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.

panels.panel_title: Objections, Indian Application and Mark-Scaled Answers
lines: CENTRAL FOCUS
Objections, Indian Application and Mark-Scaled Answers
[1] The decision-making approach can be used to analyse how an Indian policy choice
(e.g. a Cabinet or Cabinet Committee decision) moves from problem recognition to
implementation, without asserting unverified specifics of any particular real
decision unless independently confirmed.
v
[2] Objection: behavioural political science's value-neutrality claim makes it complicit
in ignoring urgent injustice, since choosing what to study/ignore is itself a
value-laden act. Reply: post-behaviouralism (Easton) does not abandon science in
response; it insists that knowledge must be made relevant and put to responsible use
while retaining verification and rigour — "action" is added to, not substituted for,
evidence standards. (PDF pp.121-122)
v
[3] The structural-functional approach can compare India's formal parliamentary
structures with informal interest-articulation channels (caste associations, kinship
networks, local patron-client ties) performing the same function in different areas
— cite this as a type of comparison, not with unverified statistics.
v
[4] Thesis: political inquiry has moved from traditional/normative approaches to a
scientific, and then a value-conscious, contemporary approach.
v
SYNTHESIS -> Objections, Indian Application and Mark-Scaled Answers is best presented through
its central claim, causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
EXAM ROUTE -> define precisely -> explain the mechanism -> test the limit ->
conclude with a qualified political judgment.
CENTRAL FOCUS
MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair
[1] Method: The procedure of inquiry by which reliable knowledge and conclusions are
obtained.
v
[2] Approach: A wider frame that includes method plus criteria for selecting problems,
questions and relevant data.
v
[3] Empirical statement: A claim about an observable situation that can be tested or
verified by repeated observation.
v
[4] Normative statement: A claim expressing a preference, duty or moral principle about
what ought to be valued or prescribed.
v
SYNTHESIS -> MCQ Remediation and Trap Repair is best presented through its central claim,
causal logic, strongest limit and qualified verdict.
